newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil expects Oct trade gap, but not huge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil expects Oct trade gap, but not huge.

text.p: The Brazilian government no longer blushes at the prospect of a trade deficit in October, but officials said they were skeptical about market projections that the gap for the month would reach $1.0 billion or more.

Noting that imports in October would have to come in at a record for the year of $5.2 billion plus to trigger such a large deficit, a senior government source involved in trade policy formulation said it was unlikely.

"We're talking a 10 percent growth month-on-month in imports for that to happen," the source said, requesting anonymity. "That's hardly likely. I can't see any reason to imagine a deficit of that magnitude ($1.0 billion in October)."
He added that should imports total some $5.2 billion for October, as predicted by some analysts, the two-way trade for the month would be on the order of $9.4 billion.
"We don't even have the infrastructure to handle trade in such volumes," he said.
The Ministry of Industry and Commerce Tuesday revealed disappointing exports of $4.188 billion in October, up from $4.115 billion in September but down from October 1995's $4.405 billion.
In September, imports were $4.77 billion, generating a deficit of $655 million, and in October last year, imports stood at $4.071 billion.
September's deficit was largely blamed on petroleum imports, which the source said were unlikely to reoccur in such volumes in October.

If petroleum imports remained high, he doubted that October would exceed September's unusually large purchases. He also believed Christmas sales would not spark as explosive a burst in imports as some analysts are foreseeing.

Finance Minister Pedro Malan, interviewed by the Jornal do Brasil newspaper, poured customary cold water on market jitters at Brazil's trade performance. "Imports are under 8.0 percent of GDP (gross domestic product), one of the lowest ratios in the world," the paper quoted him as saying.
"It's not a problem, especially if you take into account that 25 percent of imports are capital goods."

Malan said only 17-18 percent of imports were composed of consumer goods and noted that the recent exemption of exports from so-called ICMS tax and the re-creation of an export insurance agency would boost overseas sales next year.
The Finance Minister also reiterated his view that short-term worries over the trade balance were "mistaken" and that the current account situation was far more important.
"The current account deficit, which is what's relevant, is totally controllable," he said. Malan added that at least 40 percent of the gap was financed by direct foreign investment.
"We are not worried about financing a (current account) deficit of this size," he said, referring to government forecasts the gap will hit some 2.5-3.0 percent of GDP in 1996.

A spokesman for Malan said there was, as yet, no way of knowing exactly how large October's imports were. Officials had so far only gathered information from some airports and from Rio de Janeiro and Santos ports.
